newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma drags feet over budget cutting.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma drags feet over budget cutting.

text.p: Russia's parliament dragged its feet on Friday over a government plan to cut budget spending but a senior deputy suggested it might review another part of the austerity package rejected earlier.
The Communist-dominated State Duma lower house put off for the third time a vote on changes to the 1997 budget which the cabinet says are needed to sort out Russia's chaotic finances.

A special commission set up to try to overcome differences between parliament and the government failed to reach a compromise on Thursday and parliament had been due to discuss and vote on its own proposals on Friday.
But Alexander Zhukov, deputy head of the State Duma's budget committee, told parliament: "The vote on spending cuts is put on Monday's agenda at 12.30 (0830 GMT)."

The reformist government, which is facing a shortfall in tax revenues, wants to slash spending to put it in line with reality. The cabinet initially sought to cut 108 trillion roubles ($18.7 billion).
The parliament argues its long-suffering electorate would not accept the spending squeeze and wants to distance itself from the unpopular move or insist on much smaller cuts.

The prospects of winning the battle for the budget cuts has become brighter for the government since it scored a victory in a different corner on Wednesday, pushing through the Duma the first reading of its new tax code.

Young reformers brought into the government by President Boris Yeltsin to give a boost to stalled economic reforms view the new tax code as the main instrument in encouraging economic growth after years of stagnation.
The reluctant Duma approved the tax code in principle but reserved the right to fight for dramatic changes in the document during subsequent readings of the bill.
"The Duma has taken up the government's main initiatives and so far it is a draw," a senior Kremlin official told reporters on condition of anonymity.

"It would be very good to have the Duma also approve the government's social package," the official added, referring to the government's proposal to cut huge social benefits which was rejected by the Duma earlier this week.
The government has argued Russia's struggling economy cannot keep up a generous safety net of social benefits inherited from the paternalistic Soviet system.

Ministers complain more than 100 million Russians, two-thirds of the population, are theoretically eligible for different benefits worth more than 350 trillion roubles ($60 billion) a year. They say it made a nonsense of the system.

In a clear sign of changing mood, RIA news agency quoted the head of the Duma's committee for social policy, Sergei Kalashnikov, as saying there was a chance the chamber could return to the social package.
Ultra-nationalist Kalashnikov said he expected deputies to pass a compromise version of the plan which his committee would present to the chamber on Monday.
But it was not clear whether Communist deputies and other government opponents in the Duma shared Kalashnikov's optimism.
"The deputies appear uncommitted and our feeling is that the situation is quite tense," the Kremlin official said.
